title: Open Source Software

BIDS & Motion-BIDS

The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) is the community standard for organising neuroscience data. I co-led the extension for motion data, Motion-BIDS (BEP029), which covers optical motion capture, inertial sensors and other tracking systems. Today I contribute to the specification and teach BIDS in workshops and in the IGOR BIDS Consultation Hour.
motionbids is a lightweight Python package I develop for curating motion datasets in the Motion-BIDS format (documentation, PyPI).
My role: co-lead author of Motion-BIDS; developer of motionbids

KielMAT

The Kiel Motion Analysis Toolbox (KielMAT), formerly NGMT, is an open-source Python toolbox for gait and balance analysis in neurological cohorts. It runs validated algorithms on wearable and motion-capture data, and its data model is built around Motion-BIDS.
My role: co-developer and co-maintainer

title: Research
text:
The moving brain
For a long time, EEG meant sitting still. With mobile EEG we can record brain activity while people walk, turn and deal with the real world. I combine mobile EEG with motion capture, EMG and wearable sensors to study how the cortex takes part in controlling gait, for example through beta oscillations and corticomuscular coherence, and how this changes in Parkinson’s disease.
Projects: StepuP · EEGManySteps · Pocketable MoBI · EPOC

title: Research
text:
Gait, balance and foot placement
Walking is controlled step by step, largely through where we put our feet. I work on algorithms that turn raw sensor data into meaningful gait and balance parameters, and on models of how the nervous system plans foot placement under uncertainty.
Projects: Bayesian foot placement · KielMAT · StepuP

title: Research
text:
Movement disorders
Trained as a psychologist and neuroscientist, I want to understand movement disorders through quantitative data: how essential tremor responds to sensory feedback and arousal, which gait measures track the progression of Parkinson’s disease, and how mobility, cognition and clinical scores relate in geriatric patients.
Projects: StepuP · Tremor · ComOn

title: Research
text:
Open and reproducible science
Mobile EEG multiplies the analysis choices a researcher has to make. I study these choices and their consequences, develop reporting standards and data standards such as Motion-BIDS, and help build the communities that make open research the default.
Projects: META-REP · IGOR · EEGManySteps · Motion-BIDS

title: Bayesian integration in foot placement control
text:
The question
We keep our balance while walking mainly through foot placement. Where the foot lands is adjusted step by step to the state of the body’s centre of mass (CoM). In steady-state walking, a simple linear model of CoM position and velocity during swing predicts a large part of where the next foot will land. The variance it explains is taken as the degree of foot placement control, and its residuals as foot placement error (Wang & Srinivasan, 2014; Bruijn & van Dieën, 2018).
But the nervous system never knows the state of the centre of mass directly. It has to estimate it from noisy visual, vestibular and proprioceptive signals and from its own predictions. Bayesian observer models say how this should be done: weigh each source of information by its reliability, and combine the evidence with prior expectations (Ernst & Banks, 2002; Körding & Wolpert, 2004). Together with Moira van Leeuwen and the Amsterdam group, I ask whether foot placement follows these principles.

If the senses become less reliable, a Bayesian walker should rely less on the momentary state of the body, and more on what it expects.

title: Bayesian integration in foot placement control
text:
Approach
A Bayesian account makes testable predictions. If the sensory estimate of body state becomes less reliable, foot placement should depend less on the measured CoM state and shift towards prior expectations, as in the figure above. The project builds on three established lines of work:

the CoM-based foot placement model developed in Amsterdam (open-source FootPlacement code by Moira van Leeuwen and Sjoerd Bruijn; van Leeuwen et al., 2020)
earlier work that degrades specific sensory cues during walking, for example with muscle vibration (Arvin et al., 2018) or vestibular stimulation (Magnani et al., 2021)
observer models of state estimation and sensory integration in balance control (Kuo, 2005; Maeda et al., 2017)

Moira and I also work together in StepuP, where the Amsterdam work package studies whether treadmill training in Parkinson’s disease improves foot placement coordination and the estimation of the body’s state. We organised the first joint StepuP meeting at VU Amsterdam in February 2024.

title: META-REP: Replicability of mobile EEG
text:
The programme
META-REP, short for A Meta-scientific Programme to Analyse and Optimise Replicability in the Behavioural, Social, and Cognitive Sciences, is a DFG Priority Programme (SPP 2317). It brings together projects that study why findings do or do not replicate, and that develop ways to make them more robust. In Oldenburg, META-REP’s METEOR project looks at the “forking paths” of noisy, complex neural data: the many defensible analysis decisions between a raw recording and a published result. My work within META-REP is about these forking paths in mobile EEG.

title: META-REP: Replicability of mobile EEG
section: Why mobile EEG needs a reporting standard
text:
Why mobile EEG needs a reporting standard
Mobile EEG lets us study the brain while people walk, turn and navigate the real world. The price is a large space of decisions that stationary EEG rarely faces: which amplifier and cap, how cables are secured, how EEG is synchronised with motion sensors, how gait events are detected, and how movement artefacts are removed, in which order and with which parameters.
In Preprocessing on the Go we reviewed studies that combined mobile EEG with gait measurements (Vinod et al., 2026). The preprocessing steps differed widely, as did their order and combination, and especially the tools and reporting of artefact rejection. Many studies described their pipeline too vaguely to reproduce it. Our conclusion is that the field does not need one mandatory pipeline. It does need standardised reporting, so that different pipelines become comparable and studies can be repeated. An earlier META-REP review of P3 studies during walking came to a similar verdict (Jacobsen et al., 2025).

The field does not need one mandatory pipeline. It needs every pipeline to be reported well enough to repeat.

title: META-REP: Replicability of mobile EEG
section: A reporting standard for mobile EEG
text:
A reporting standard for mobile EEG
The cornerstone of my META-REP work is a reporting standard for mobile EEG studies, now in preparation: a shared minimum of what a paper reports, so that readers can evaluate, compare and repeat it. Its starting point is what the review found missing most often:


Recording context Setting and task, such as indoor or outdoor, treadmill or overground walking, and the equipment used.
Preprocessing steps Every step with its order and tools, in particular how movement artefacts are rejected.
Software parameters The settings of each tool, so that a pipeline can be re-run.
Open code and workflows Analysis code and workflows shared openly, ideally with data in community standards such as EEG-BIDS and Motion-BIDS.

title: META-REP: Replicability of mobile EEG
text:
Related work

EEGManySteps: a many-labs effort that measures how much setups and pipelines change gait-related EEG results.
IGOR umbrella review: a review of how EEG/ERP preprocessing is reported and justified across the literature.
Multiverse analyses: mapping preprocessing choices in mobile EEG and a multiverse of beta activity during gait by Vaishali Vinod. The first maps the choices made in the literature (Oldenburg METEOR team); the second varies preprocessing choices on two walking datasets.

title: EEGManySteps
text:
The idea
EEGManySteps is a grassroots initiative in mobile brain/body imaging (MoBI). It is not a classic replication study. Instead, it collects and harmonises walking EEG recorded with many different setups around the world, both existing datasets and new recordings, to find out which acquisition and analysis factors most affect how consistent and reliable gait-related EEG results are.
The community settled on four research goals:

step-specific time-frequency patterns,
gait-related artefacts across EEG systems,
the influence of preprocessing on EEG results during walking, and
gait-related modulation of secondary-task correlates such as the P3.

title: EEGManySteps
text:
Harmonised data
Contributed datasets are converted to EEG-BIDS and Motion-BIDS. They also get EEGManySteps metadata: indoor or outdoor, treadmill or overground, footwear, secondary task, speed scheme and synchronisation method. Sensor locations follow the UNISEP sensor-placement vocabulary, and gait events are standardised. For new recordings, the project shares a harmonised auditory oddball paradigm that can be run while standing and while walking.

title: StepuP: Steps against the burden of Parkinson’s disease
text:
The question
Speed-dependent treadmill training improves gait in Parkinson’s disease, but nobody knows the mechanism. StepuP tests two candidate explanations. The first is that training sharpens stability-related foot placement, the step-by-step adjustment of where the foot lands relative to the body’s centre of mass. The second is that it strengthens cortical sensorimotor integration, visible as lower gait-related EEG beta power and higher EEG–EMG (corticomuscular) coherence. A second question is whether a richer training regime (SDTT+, with virtual reality or mechanical perturbations) works better, and whether the gains carry over into walking in daily life.

Speed-dependent treadmill training helps. StepuP is designed to find out how, from the cortex down to the foot.

title: StepuP: Steps against the burden of Parkinson’s disease
text:
Design
StepuP consists of three harmonised, parallel randomised controlled trials that share one core protocol and run at clinical sites in Kiel, Bologna, Tel Aviv and Sydney. Each trial includes 42 people with Parkinson’s disease, so 126 in total. A reference group of 21 healthy older adults is measured in Amsterdam. Participants are randomised to standard speed-dependent treadmill training (SDTT) or to SDTT+, and complete twelve 30-minute training sessions. Depending on the site, SDTT+ adds virtual-reality obstacles, mechanical belt perturbations, or both.
Assessments take place at baseline, right after training and at a 12-week follow-up. Each one combines:

Synchronised 64-channel EEG, EMG and 3D motion capture during treadmill walking at comfortable and fixed speeds, plus resting-state EEG
Clinical testing, e.g. MDS-UPDRS III, Mini-BESTest, MoCA, Trail Making Test, Timed Up and Go, falls self-efficacy and quality of life
A week of daily-life monitoring with a lower-back motion sensor, which yields real-world digital mobility outcomes

The primary clinical endpoint is comfortable overground walking speed. Mechanistic outcomes include stride length and stride time, the explained variance and error of a foot-placement model, EEG beta power and corticomuscular coherence. They are analysed with linear mixed-effects models.

title: StepuP: Steps against the burden of Parkinson’s disease
text:
Data that travel well
A multicentre study with different EEG, EMG and motion-capture systems at every site only works if the data line up. All sites stream and time-lock their devices with the open-source Lab Streaming Layer. The recordings are then converted into one multi-site dataset in the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS), with eeg, emg and motion data for every participant and session. This is where Motion-BIDS proves itself in practice.

Together with Walter Maetzler, I lead StepuP at the Kiel site (University Hospital Schleswig-Holstein and Kiel University), where we supervise the team running the EEG, EMG, motion-capture and training sessions. Across the consortium I am responsible for the multimodal recording and data-standardisation pipeline:

the LSL synchronisation setup for the EEG, EMG and motion-capture systems used at the sites

What IGOR does
IGOR is a forum where members of the DGPs section Biological Psychology and Neuropsychology exchange ideas on how to make research in the field more open and reproducible. It works through grassroots community projects, training for early-career researchers and the annual IGOR Prize for Open and Reproducible Science. Its founding document (in German) is available here.

title: IGOR: Interest Group on Open and Reproducible Research
text:
BIDS Consultation Hour
In 2024 I set up the IGOR BIDS Consultation Hour, an open online forum. Researchers bring their own datasets and conversion problems and get individual advice on organising them in the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS). I cover EEG and motion data, and a colleague covers MRI. The website also collects BIDS learning materials, such as workshop slides and posters.

title: IGOR: Interest Group on Open and Reproducible Research
text:
EEG/ERP preprocessing umbrella review
Together with Yu-Fang Yang, Mario Reutter-Dieker and Johannes Rodrigues, I co-lead an umbrella review of EEG/ERP preprocessing practices. It brings together the literature on how preprocessing pipelines and parameters are reported and justified. The aim is a shared, transparent set of extraction standards and evidence the field can reuse. The review is preregistered on OSF and complements my work on reporting standards for mobile EEG.
